title: Rebellion in Euphrates Delta
detail: A ninth-century rebellion during the Abbasid caliphate by thousands of enslaved East Africans working on cane fields in the Euphrates Delta.

title: Three pounds of sugar
detail: King Henry III of England pays what would amount to roughly US$450 today for three pounds of sugar, before sugar is common among the non-elite in Western Europe.

title: Black Death
detail: The Black Death (1347–1351) drastically reduces peasant labour in Europe and the Mediterranean; rulers of Sicily, Cyprus, Rhodes and Crete import enslaved people from North Africa instead of corvée labour.

title: Columbus reaches the Americas
detail: Christopher Columbus (1451–1506); genocide of Indigenous peoples of the Americas and Caribbean follows. Bartolomé de las Casas, who sailed on Columbus's third voyage, later calls Columbus a murderer and rapist.

title: Magellan
detail: Ferdinand Magellan (1480–1521); 'Age of Discovery'.

title: Vasco da Gama
detail: Vasco da Gama (c. 1460–1524) sails around Africa to Asia; his rampage and mass murder documented by Sanjay Subrahmanyam.

title: Treaty of Tordesillas
detail: 1494 line 'drawn on a map' dividing the world between Spain and Portugal; Portuguese then strengthen claims to Brazil with land grants worked by enslaved labour after genocidal violence against Indigenous people.

title: Expulsion from Iberia
detail: King Manuel I expels Sephardic Jews and Arabs from Iberia, removing the merchant-finance communities that had provided capital and marketing for Mediterranean sugar.

title: First asiento
detail: The asiento — a licence from the Spanish Crown authorising traders to sell enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies — is first issued. Until 1595 it is a contract of any nationality to import a specified number in return for royalty; destinations include Bolivian and Mexican silver mines.

title: Spanish silver dollar
detail: Mid-sixteenth-century 'real de a ocho' ('piece of eight'): commodity money accepted across Asia, the Americas and Europe; 80% of world silver supply 1494–1850 comes from Mexico and Potosí.

title: Historia de las Indias
detail: Bartolomé de las Casas' Historia de Las Indias (published 1875) documents colonial violence in the Indies.

title: Asiento opened to any nationality
detail: From 1595 the asiento is no longer limited to Spanish subjects.

title: Dutch Essequibo
detail: Dutch establish colonies on the Guiana coast including Essequibo; Suriname later becomes Dutch Guiana.

title: Dutch seize northern Brazil
detail: 1624–1654: Dutch gain control of Portugal's plantations in northern Brazil (Pernambuco), learn sugar-plantation techniques, then spread production to Caribbean colonies; expelled by Portuguese in 1654.

title: England claims Barbados
detail: England claims Barbados in 1625 and begins settlement in 1627; sugar then adopted by British planters.

title: French Guadeloupe & Martinique
detail: France establishes colonies in Guadeloupe and Martinique; French planters adopt the Dutch sugar-plantation model.

title: Dutch capture Elmina Castle
detail: In 1637 the Dutch capture Elmina Castle in present-day Ghana, a major centre for purchasing, confining and shipping enslaved Africans; seized with Portuguese trade in enslaved people.

title: England seizes Jamaica
detail: England seizes Jamaica from Spain in 1655; Kingston becomes a hub of the trade in enslaved people.

title: Great Plague of London
detail: Sugar refineries relocate from London to other English ports; West Indian ships use other docks to avoid contagion, expanding sugar refining across Britain.

title: Barbados windmills
detail: About 400 pairs of wings turn crushing rollers in Barbados by 1670; windmills survive the Industrial Revolution — 219 sugar estates in Barbados still wind-powered on the eve of World War I.

title: Dutch secure the asiento
detail: Dutch secure the asiento; Amsterdam near-monopolises European sugar refining and ~20% of the trade in enslaved people to the Americas; Dutch guilder becomes Atlantic reserve currency, backed by the Bank of Amsterdam.

title: Jamaica sugar to Britain
detail: Between 1682 and 1701 Britain is the destination for more than 95% of Jamaica's sugar exports.

title: Asiento to Dutch
detail: Spanish Crown grants the asiento to the Dutch (1685), French (1702), then British South Sea Company (1713–1739).

title: Treaty of Rijswijk
detail: France gains the western third of Hispaniola, renamed Saint-Domingue (now Haiti); 'by the second half of the eighteenth century Britain and France are the major colonial presence in the Caribbean.'

title: Barbados sugar share
detail: Sugar products account for 91.2% of Barbados' total exports 1665–1666, 91.6% in 1688 & 1690–1691, 95.6% in 1699–1701 (David Eltis).

title: Asiento to French
detail: Asiento granted to the French.

title: British South Sea Company
detail: British South Sea Company granted the asiento 1713–1739, teaming with the Crown-owned Royal Africa Company; Britain dominates the enslaved trade from the 1740s.

title: Jamaican enslaved population rises
detail: Between 1720s and 1788 the enslaved population in Jamaica's five leading sugar parishes increases more than sixfold; peak arrivals in the prosperous early 1790s.

title: Indian textiles to West Africa
detail: 1750–1850: British and French East India Companies ship Indian textiles to West Africa to exchange for enslaved people; Indian saltpetre → gunpowder → exchanged for enslaved Africans; land revenue from Indian peasants pays for exports.

title: Jamaica factor concentration
detail: 28 Sep 1751 – 27 May 1752: 31 ships carrying 7,123 enslaved Africans arrive in Jamaica; sale concentrated in nine factor firms; three firms handle 83%.

title: Battle of Plassey
detail: British victory at Plassey; Britain stops sending silver to India, paying for textiles from Indian land taxes; later sells forcibly grown Indian opium to China.

title: Thomas Hibbert
detail: 1764–1774: 'slave factor' Thomas Hibbert handles cargo for 61 ships and 16,254 enslaved Africans; co-founds London firm Hibbert, Purrier & Horton.

title: 40% of British capital
detail: Stanley Engerman estimate: in 1770 close to 40% of capital for Britain's commercial and industrial expansion derives from profits of the enslaved trade; sugar + slavery profits ~5% of British national income; colonial investments 4–7× more profitable.

title: Raw sugar a fifth of British imports
detail: Raw sugar accounts for one-fifth of all British imports, surpassing all other imported goods; Jamaica's enslaved-population value ~£25 million ≈ total recorded wealth 1774.

title: William Cowper's anti-slavery poem
detail: 'Pity for Poor Africans', satirical anti-slavery poem printed and distributed in 1788 by the Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade.

title: Surplus equals subsistence
detail: Klas Rönnbäck: surplus appropriated by Jamaican plantation owners rises from 40% of subsistence costs in 1750 to 100% in 1790; 4× price difference muscovado (Jamaica) vs refined sugar (England) suggests transfer pricing.

title: Sevenfold sugar imports
detail: British sugar imports rise sevenfold 1700–1800: 430,000 hundredweight (~21,845 t) → 3,000,000 hundredweight (~152,407 t); sugar production in Americas 50,000 → 200,000 tonnes; planter receipts ×3.2 since 1713.

title: British abolition of the trade
detail: Trade in enslaved people banned in Britain; British transatlantic slave trade 1640–1807 forcibly transports ~3.1 million Africans (~2.7 million survive the crossing).

title: Centrifuges
detail: Centrifuges introduced in the 1830s reduce separation of molasses from sugar from months in clay cones to hours; quickly standard even on enslaved-labour plantations.

title: Opium Wars
detail: 1839–1860 Opium Wars; Britain sells forcibly grown Indian opium to China to reverse the silver deficit.

title: Silver share
detail: Silver mined in Spanish America (Mexico, Potosí) accounts for 80% of world silver supply 1494–1850.
